H1.text: A fast fan looks like a blurred disc. A bee keeps buzzing around one flower. A swing in a night photo becomes a smooth smear.

H2.text: In each one, we cannot follow the thing itself. We only see where it is likely to be.

H3.text: Diya sees it in her kitchen. Steam rises from the cooker. She cannot follow one droplet, only the shape of the cloud.

H4.text: Electrons are like that. We cannot track one, so chemists draw the shape of the space where it is likely to be.

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will know why a p orbital looks like a dumbbell, with nothing at its centre.

P1.text: So what does an orbital look like?

P2.text: Imagine marking a dot at every place the electron might be. Where the dots are thick, the chance is high. This chance is the probability density, written psi squared.

P3.text: Now draw a boundary that holds about ninety percent of the dots. This is a boundary surface diagram. It gives the shape of the orbital.

S1.text: Let's see the shapes on our molecule bench. Start with s orbitals.

S2.text: One s is a sphere around the nucleus. Drawn flat, it looks like a circle. Every direction is the same.

S3.text: Two s is a bigger sphere. But inside it, there is a thin shell where the chance of finding the electron is zero. That is a node.

S4.text: A node shaped like a sphere is a radial node. Two s has one radial node. Three s has two.

S5.text: Now p orbitals. Each one has two lobes, one on each side of the nucleus, like a dumbbell.

S6.text: Between the lobes is a flat plane through the nucleus, where the chance is zero. This is an angular node, also called a nodal plane.

S7.text: There are three p orbitals, along x, y and z. Same size, same shape and same energy. They differ only in direction.

S8.text: Next, d orbitals. For l equals two, there are five of them. The first four look like four leaf clovers.

S9.text: In d x y, d y z and d z x, the lobes lie between the axes. In d x squared minus y squared, the lobes lie on the axes.

S10.text: The fifth, d z squared, looks different. Two lobes along z, with a ring around the middle. Still, all five three d orbitals have the same energy.

B1.text: Now look at two s and two p. Each one has exactly one node.

B2.text: Pause and think. Which one has a radial node, shaped like a sphere?

B3.text: Two s. Its node is a sphere. Two p has a flat plane through the nucleus instead. That is an angular node.

D1.text: So how many nodes does an orbital have? Let's count, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Angular nodes, the flat ones, equal l. So s has zero, p has one, and d has two.

D3.text: Step two. Radial nodes, the round ones, equal n minus l minus one.

D4.text: Step three. Add them. l plus n minus l minus one gives n minus one. That is the total number of nodes.

D5.text: Step four. Check two p. Radial, two minus one minus one, is zero. Angular is one. Total one, which is two minus one.

T1.text: Remember this. Angular nodes equal l. Radial nodes equal n minus l minus one.

W2.text: Count the nodes of a three d orbital, and a four p orbital.

W3.text: Three d. n is three and l is two. Angular nodes, two. Radial nodes, three minus two minus one, zero.

W4.text: So all the nodes of three d are flat planes. Total two, which is three minus one.

W5.text: Four p. n is four and l is one. Angular nodes, one. Radial nodes, four minus one minus one, two.

W6.text: Total three, which is four minus one. Both answers check.

X2.text: Many students say radial nodes equal n minus one. So they give two p one radial node.

X3.text: But n minus one is the total. Radial nodes are n minus l minus one. Two p has no radial node. Its only node is the flat plane.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main, as counting radial and angular nodes, or naming the orbital from its nodes.

Q1.text: Exam level now. An orbital has two radial nodes and one angular node. Which orbital is it? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Four p.

A2.text: One angular node means l equals one. So it is a p orbital.

A3.text: Radial nodes are n minus l minus one, which is two. So n minus two equals two, and n is four.

A4.text: Four p. Option A, three p, has only one radial node.

Y2.text: One. What shape is an s orbital, and how does it change from one s to two s?

Y3.text: Two. How many angular nodes does a d orbital have?

Y4.text: Three. How many radial nodes does a three s orbital have?

N1.text: Next time: three d and four s are close in energy, so which one fills first? We find out in Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule.
